IMr. Martin (Essex East).]

Mr. Speaker, the members of the Vancouver city council called upon me to discuss questions relating to the operation of the Vancouver international airport by the city of Vancouver and the method of financing a new terminal building there.
I informed the delegation that government policy provided for grants in aid to terminal buildings at municipal airports served by class 1 scheduled services. The amount of the grant in aid would be related to the cost of the customs and immigration space, and a proportion of the public waiting room space in the building. I also informed them it would not be possible to go beyond this policy or to have the federal government finance the whole of the construction of the terminal building, either by loan to the city

Members of the delegation also inquired regarding the responsibility for the operation of the airfield, and I informed them that we were quite happy with the present efficient operation of the airfield, but that if at any time the city felt that it wished the federal government to take over full responsibility for operation, this was a matter we would be prepared to discuss with the appropriate municipal authorities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, an amendment was moved last night to this subclause which is now under consideration. That amendment would have incorporated in this bill the provisions of paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of section 14 and subsection 2 of section 14 of the Railway Act. This refers to the fact that no commissioner or officer of the board-that is, the board of transport commissioners-should have any interest, if I may paraphrase it, in stocks, shares, bonds, debentures or other securities of any company that comes under that act.
Our consideration of that amendment may be summed up as follows. The purpose of a provision such as subclause 5 is to ensure that the board will be disinterested and unbiased. In drafting such a provision as this it is not easy to cover all conceivable cases, as hon. members will understand, and the danger is that the provision will go too far. In the Railway Act there is no disqualification in a case where a member of the board is a director or other officer, as there is in the present bill. Moreover, the Railway Act prohibits a member of the board from indirectly being interested in any security of a company. Read literally, this would prohibit a member of the board from holding a participating life insurance policy with a company that had invested some of its funds in securities of a railway company.
In the present bill we have tried to draft a provision that would cover the normal cases without, at the same time, leading to

absurd situations. There is an important distinction between this clause and the present provision in the Railway Act, in that under the Railway Act there is only an obligation to report and get rid of an interest, whereas in the present bill there is an absolute statutory disqualification. I should think the present provision is wide enough to dissuade any member from being interested in bonds or securities of a company, because if he transgressed the section he would by operation of law become disqualified. It must also be borne in mind that the proposed board is to be a court of record, and it is a fundamental principle, whether stated in the statute or not, that a judicial tribunal must be unbiased.
I do not expect there will be any difficulty in applying this section so as to disqualify all those who ought to be disqualified, and I am therefore unable to accept the amendment that has been moved.

We gave very serious consideration to the subject matter which the hon. member has drawn to the attention of the committee. Our judgment was that the way we have set it out in the bill would be a satisfactory method of dealing with these problems of appeal. We considered the Railway Act, and we have had experience with regard to the type of appeal which emerges from the method outlined in that act. We considered that the new board, dealing as it will with highly complicated and technical matters, should have its findings thereon considered to be conclusive. Other matters of law and jurisdiction are, of course, dealt with in the normal manner.
As we have just discussed with reference to an earlier section, the board is empowered to make changes and review its decisions if new evidence is produced on the basis of some complaint by an individual, and we feel that in matters as highly technical as those which are involved in dealing with the problems that will face the energy board it would be better and more in the interests of the public if the board's findings of fact were held to be final and conclusive.
Very careful consideration has been given to this question, and we think it should be left in this way. If subsequent experience shows that something more should be done, parliament will have an opportunity to consider the matter. The question has been gone into with the greatest of care and we have concluded that this is a satisfactory method.

One of the strangest arguments that we heard was from the Minister of Public Works who said that if the board should undertake an inquiry into atomic energy it was something that would not be published or should not be published. I should like to criticize that statement on two grounds. First of all, I do not think it is the intention of this bill-and the minister can say whether or not this is correct-to have the board inquiring into the field of atomic energy and making reports about atomic energy. The second thing-and this is even more discouraging-is the attitude of the government that any inquiry into the field of atomic energy is something that should be kept a state secret. This is greatly overdone. The scientific

National Energy Board facts about atomic energy are not only available to Canada but to all of the countries of the world. This represents more a state of mind on the part of the government than anything based on any sound argument or any real fact.
Another argument that we have had advanced-this has already been dealt with a number of times; a completely fallacious argument-is that this has to be secret, or the provisions for keeping it secret must remain, because the board might be inquiring into something under provincial jurisdiction. This is a rather strange attitude for the government to take. First of all, I do not know why under clause 22 the board would be inquiring into things that are under provincial jurisdiction because it specifically states that:
The board shall study and keep under review matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction-
Why would the board be wandering into the fields of provincial jurisdiction? Then, there is the further qualifying phrase in the same subclause:
-as it considers necessary or advisable in the public interest-
Surely, these two provisions make it necessary that all of these reports should be made public. We are having a great deal of difficulty I would think, Mr. Chairman, in dealing with this measure because we are getting answers from so many people. The bill is in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This is what the bill says, but some of the questions are answered by the Minister of Public Works, some are answered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the advice of the Minister of Justice who was sitting with him part of the time this morning, and then we have a couple of candidates for parliamentary secretaryships, or potential parliamentary secretaries, competing one with the other and with the minister in the field of answering questions. In that event, of course, the only way by which information could be given out would be by interrogation in this house, by voluntary statement in the house or outside by the minister.

The minister, as a lawyer, knows that what is said in these debates will not assist in any way those who have to interpret what this clause means after the bill has become law. The courts, in interpreting these clauses, are not permitted, under the rules of evidence and interpretation, to ascertain the meaning of a clause by observing what took place at the time the particular clause was adopted in the legislature. The good intentions of the minister, therefore, will not help future litigants or others concerned.
In any event while the minister himself may have the best of intentions and may intend that written reports shall be tabled provided they are not contrary to the public interest, he is not a unique creation of the Creator endowed with immortality, in terms of his person and in terms of his particular tenure. Next week he may become the minister of external affairs, for instance; I do not know. His successor is not likely to have the same good intentions that my hon. friend has. I suggest to him that while I appreciate, as one who has piloted measures through parliament, the reluctance of a minister to see his own special creation emasculated beyond the proportions that he, himself, had devised, I suggest to him that the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition, which really represents a compromise from the original amendment, is one to which the minister, in pursuing his present interest, ought to accede.

The question which was asked me was with regard to possible duplication of effort, and I think reference was made to recommendation No. 18 of the Borden report. That recommendation reads as follows:
That such divisions or branches of the various departments of the government of Canada now concerned with oil and natural gas related matters and whose responsibilities would properly come within the jurisdiction of the national energy board be transferred to its jurisdiction.
The question concerned the number of divisions within government circles which would have some responsibility to these and related matters. It was considered rather difficult to express a transfer of these functions in legislative terms and that after the energy board was set up the departments which were concerned with studies similar to those to be conducted by the energy board would review their position and see whether or not their activities would be curtailed in any respect. I had a search made of the various departments of government and crown corporations that have some work going on related to that which will be undertaken by the energy board, and if the committee would like a list of them I am quite prepared to give it. They are arranged alphabetically.
First of all there is, as has been mentioned, the atomic energy control board. Then Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which does research and standards on domestic heating. The defence production department on its purchasing side has something to do with sources of energy. Then there is the dominion bureau of statistics, naturally. The external affairs department has a function to perform, or at least an interest in the licensing function of the national energy board, where international movement of energy and energy sources is concerned. The finance department naturally has an interest in the national energy board, but not in the research side of it. The

National Energy Board international joint commission, as was mentioned in the Borden commission report, will be doing work which will be of interest to the national energy board concerning the export of electricity. The mines and technical surveys department indicates considerable activity in fields which are related to those that the energy board will be surveying.
The national defence department is concerned only with regard to the question of fuels for their purposes. The national research council does quite a bit of work with regard to building research which has to do with heating appliances. Of course, the national revenue department exercises control with regard to imports and exports under its customs and excise division. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is active in research matters on energy and requirements through its economics division, water resources branch, and mining and lands division. The northern Canada power commission puts forward policies regarding production of power in northern Canada and the maritimes. The Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation might perhaps be considered as an interested party here. The tariff board would be interested in policy matters regarding import controls.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has its energy studies branch, a branch which has been largely responsible for the immense amount of work which had to be done prior to the introduction of this bill. The standards branch is interested in the export of electrical power and exports and imports of gas. The chemicals division of the commodities branch has an interest in petrochemicals and oil and gas; and of course the department generally in connection with external trade. The board of transport commissioners, as I mentioned in the earlier stages of the debate, will transfer its duties to the national energy board and be concerned only with instances where pipe lines cross railway lines. The Department of Transport will obviously have an interest in matters of transportation of energy and sources of energy when consulted by the national energy board.
Those are the areas in which there might be some duplication of effort, but chiefly I would think it would lie in the work now being done by the mines and technical surveys department and the northern affairs and national resources department. I think if any overlapping will occur, it will occur there. Experience will show to what extent some of that work might be continued under those departments, and what part of it might rather be performed by the national energy board and the information obtained by that board made available to these departments which are interested.

Mr. Chairman, the minister
has answered by giving a long list of departments and agencies which are concerned with energy and sources of energy. That shows there may be a duplication, as the minister has said, and I think we should try to avoid this.
The minister said before, I think in the debate on second reading, that it was not the intention of parliament to incorporate those agencies in this new organization, and we are all in favour of that. We want the board to operate separately and we want some other agencies to operate separately. The question is how much duplication there will be, how much expansive operation there will be due to the fact that this board is authorized to do research and investigation, and so on, on all matters concerning energy and sources of energy.
I think this should be clarified. For instance, how would the dominion coal board be related to the energy board? This we should know, because coal is a source of energy. We should also like to know how the international joint commission will be related to this new board, and how the atomic energy control board will be related to this new agency. What about the water resources branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and any other departments which are concerned? I think this should be clarified, and for this reason I wish to propose an amendment to clause 22 subsection 1 which reads as follows:
That subsection 1 of clause 22 be amended by addition of the following words in line 20 after the words "sources of energy":
"for which the board has regulatory responsibility."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I appreciate the hon.
member's interest in this matter and his desire, which coincides with our own, that there shall be no unnecessary duplication of duties and, as a result, added expenses. I am pleased that the hon. member introduced the word "regulatory", because there is a sharp distinction between the functions of the board in its regulatory and in its advisory duties. Here we are dealing with the board's advisory functions, and if this amendment were accepted those advisory functions would be restricted to areas in which the board has regulatory responsibility, that is, electricity, gas and oil.
Our conception of the advisory function of the board is much wider than that. We are hoping that the national energy board will keep under review all the sources of energy in this country and that its review would range over the entire field. This would not interfere with the work presently being done by the dominion coal board-we gave that

careful consideration-nor would it interfere with the work of the other bodies which have been mentioned. The energy board would, for example, draw upon the information available to the dominion coal board in order subsequently to advise the government and thence parliament as to the part coal would play in the over-all picture of the use of the energy resources of this country. Similarly, the entire field of energy would be subject to study and review by the energy board without interference with duties now being performed by the dominion coal board or Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the research council and so on. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that the information available from these bodies should be studied by the national energy board which would consolidate that information, review it and, on that basis, make recommendations and give advice.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I can appreciate the point which the minister is making, but inevitably the information which he has just given us does show the variety of government agencies engaged in these fields of energy and underlines, surely, the danger of duplication and overlapping with resultant confusion and, perhaps, unnecessary duplication and expense. The minister is no doubt aware of the operation of Parkinson's law as applied to government procedure and there is the danger-and it is a human danger-that the new energy board when set up will be subject to the temptation to carry on its investigations and researches into every field of energy, because that is what it is authorized to do by clause 22(1). There is no limitation on its activities. The men responsible for this board will be men of ability and initiative, and they will naturally wish to extend their researches into all fields of energy. That, surely, involves the danger of duplication, because there are boards which have been operating in this field for a long time, charged with duties which they have been carrying out effectively.
We have been concerned about this danger as, no doubt, has the minister himself, and if the amendment which we have suggested is not considered suitable for the purpose I wonder what steps the government visualizes as being suitable? Will the energy board be given supervisory control over all researches in this field or is there to be an intergovernmental committee which will include representatives from all the main bodies to ensure that duplication of effort and expense will not take place.

speechtext:
Clause 44 sets out under what conditions, and for what reasons, the board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line. The board will have regard to the following: The availability of oil or gas; the existence of markets; the economic feasibility; the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, and the public interest that, in the board's opinion, may be affected by the granting or the refusing of the application.
I should like to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that there should be one further condition placed in this clause which would provide for control by Canadians of the companies to which certificates may be issued. This is a proposal that, in the past, has been very dear to the hearts of hon. members opposite, namely that in the construction of gas pipe lines in particular these companies involved should be Canadian companies and should be controlled in this country.
It should almost be unnecessary to set forth the reasons why it is preferable to have a Canadian company. We see to a growing and alarming extent the further alienation of Canadian resources to outside interests and capital. The government has said in this legislation that it welcomes both foreign and Canadian capital; but even if that is the position which the government takes, I think that the interests of companies erecting pipe lines should be Canadian.
For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I would like to move the following amendment:
That clause 44 be amended by adding the following:
"Provided that no certificate shall be issued to an applicant of which less than 51 per cent of the common stock is owned by residents of Canada or by companies deemed by the board to be controlled in Canada."
We remember a previous debate, a particular pipe line debate, in which the position of the government party, which at that time was in opposition, was that the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company should be Canadian-controlled. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, because we are interested in having the
National Energy Board greatest amount of control by Canadians of Canadian industries and natural resources, we feel that this amendment should commend itself to the house. We have before us the report of the royal commission on energy. It shows to what a very large extent the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company is controlled by outside interests. Surely hon. members opposite would agree that this company is an example of the type of company which has the type of control against which we should guard. This provision does not, of course, imply public ownership; it merely states that in the development by private companies of oil and gas pipe lines certificates shall be issued only to companies wherein 51 per cent of the common stock is owned by residents of Canada, or by companies deemed by the board to be controlled in Canada. This would remove Canadian pipe line companies from control by Texas buccaneers or other kinds of buccaneers outside this country. We hope, Mr. Chairman, that the government will give sympathetic consideration to this amendment.

That latter phrase is new in legislation. The board is instructed by this clause to take full account of those matters, and particularly the opportunity for Canadians to participate. We thought that that was reasonable under the circumstances and that the board,

National Energy Board with this guidance and its public hearings, would certainly be able to discover to what extent Canadians were given an opportunity to participate. Our conclusion was that with that written into the act it would not be necessary to state any specific percentage of stock that should be owned by Canadians. Rather let us wait for some experience in the operation of the board and then we will be guided. I am not suggesting that I have any further action in mind at all. I am simply suggesting that experience is helpful in all these matters, and we have gone a long way here in publicly declaring the policy of the government-and I hope it will receive the approval of parliament-that Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in these operations.
As I say, that is new. It is different from what has prevailed in the past and should provide the opportunities that we all hope there will be for Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, my reply to that would be this, that the committee should be entitled to a more definite indication of what the government's policy is as set forth in this clause. I asked that very simple question because of the fact that according to the first line of the clause the board may do certain things subject to the approval of the governor in council. It would seem to me that since the authority of the governor in council is required for the issuance of a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line, the governor in council now must have some idea of what it means by subclause (d) to which the minister has referred, namely:
-the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line;-
I would say, Mr. Chairman, that as this clause now stands it is very nebulous, and indefinite. It is the kind of legislation that we find this government presenting to parliament more and more frequently. It is legislation that can mean all things to all people. I can imagine some American coming to see the government and asking what subclause (d) means, the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity. He might easily get the answer, "Well, of course, there have been long debates about this in the past and it reads nicely for some people but we are not going to be very difficult about the extent; we are not really too concerned whether or not Canadians have the chance to obtain a very large proportion of the control of such a company." This is completely indefinite, as I say. The extent might be zero.


There is no guarantee that it means anything more than zero, because there is no definition whatsoever.
One does not even find such a word as "substantially". Merely "the extent to which". And then it goes on: "the extent to which Canadians would have the opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line." Nothing is said about control. Nothing is said about what proportion of the voting stock should be in the hands of Canadians. This very general and inexact clause really does not tie the government to any policy at all. It is so general that it may not carry out even the hint which is provided that Canadians may have some opportunity to participate in the financing, engineering and construction of lines.
As it now reads this is a most unsatisfactory clause. It does nothing to carry out policies which members of the Conservative party advocated when in opposition, because even without this clause Canadians could probably have some opportunity to participate in the financing, engineering and construction of many of these projects. The governor in council, with the requirement that their approval must be obtained before a certificate is issued under this nebulous clause, could completely overlook the need for Canadian participation in financing, construction and engineering, to say nothing about the control of the company involved.
This is the type of loose amendment that we see so often from this government. It is most inexact; it means all things to all people, and the Canadian citizen, reading it, will have no idea what is behind the government's move to include it in this bill. I think we require something more from the minister by way of a definite statement. I should like him to comment on what the objective of the government would be as to Canadian participation in the financing, engineering and construction of pipe lines. Surely the minister owes it to the committee to say whether or not the government feels that Canadians should play a substantial part in the financing of these projects. "Substantial" is a generous word, but it means something more than zero. To what extent will there be Canadian participation in the construction of the line and so on?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This clause is, of course, one of the most important in the bill. There were certain observations made about this

portion of the bill during second reading which seemed to convey a wrong impression of what the clause could or could not do. It was argued by the Prime Minister when he was discussing the powers of the board that this clause ensured that there would be just and reasonable tolls, a matter of great importance. The Prime Minister also argued that this particular clause ensured that profits could not by any stretch of imagination be promoted which would be exorbitant or which would be extraordinarily high. Those were the words he used.
In fact, the clause makes no such provision. I cannot go as far as the hon. member for Assiniboia in arguing that there should be unreasonably restrictive provisions in a clause of this kind, for instance in respect of stock ownership by Canadian nationals. Our position on that matter has been consistent over the years and while we would naturally support any reasonable move which would assure for Canadians a maximum of control over Canadian activities, there are provisions in legislation which would be unnecessarily and unwisely restrictive and which would prevent the very kind of Canadian national development which they might purport to encourage. Nevertheless, while that kind of provision does not seem to us to be wise, to give the impression that this particular clause is an assurance that the board will take certain action and be able to prevent extraordinarily high profits being made or high tolls being charged is not justified by the language of the clause, because as I read it it is purely permissive in character. The words are: the board may do certain things. It is provided that the board shall take into account all such matters as to it appear to be relevant. And without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the board may have regard to various criteria which are set out, and which it may take into account in issuing a certificate in respect of a pipe line.
All this clause does, and we might as well be perfectly clear about it, is to advise the board that there are certain criteria which the legislation specifies which may be taken into consideration. A few moments ago the minister mentioned some of them- financial responsibility and the financial structure of the applicant, the method of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity to participate in the financing, engineering and construction of the line. There is nothing in this clause which could possibly be interpreted by the board as an instruction to do anything. It is purely permissive in character, and while these may be very useful and a valuable criteria-criteria which the board,
National Energy Board no doubt, may take into consideration-it is quite wrong to give the impression as the Prime Minister did the other day that this particular clause will ensure that tolls will not be exorbitantly high or that profits will not be extraordinarily great. I thought I would bring this matter to the consideration of the committee so that there would be no misunderstanding as to the exact meaning of this particular clause.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: We were just asking ourselves what was the exact meaning of the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition. It seemed to us he was getting forward into the other clauses which deal with tolls and tariffs. Here we are simply dealing with the issue of certificates and the considerations that are to be taken into account at the time the issue of a certificate is being considered by the board. Here we have set out the criteria that are necessary for the board to examine. I note that in looking back at the Prime Minister's speech on Tuesday, May 26 he commented upon this and listed the essential elements that appear in clause 44. We feel that this has no relationship to some of the matters to which the Leader of the Opposition has been referring. It is the issue of the certificate after the board has satisfied itself that the company making application is in a position to perform the functions that it considers it is able to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce have special reference to the observations made by the Leader of the Opposition. On a strict technical interpretation, part of what my hon. friend has said would have validity but the Leader of the Opposition, of course, was using clause 44 to make a general observation. If he had confined his remarks only to tolls, of course, he would have waited until he had reached part 4 with clauses 50 and following clauses, but he was just making a general observation prompted by the statement made by the Prime Minister as reported at page 4022 of Hansard of May 26 in which among other things the Prime Minister said:
That is one of the most important considerations, the determination of just and reasonable tolls, not tolls that by any stretch of the imagination could permit of exorbitant or extraordinarily great profits without risk being attached-
There is nothing in this particular clause or in any clause of the bill that warrants that statement. That is the gist of what the Leader of the Opposition was saying. He was recalling to hon. gentlemen opposite their observations made on another occasion. We have been looking for an opportunity of ascertaining whether in any clause of this bill there was

National Energy Board any provision that would prevent what hon. gentlemen have so frequently referred to on other occasions. This is the opportunity for them to implement these statements and allegations of another day.
We were told not long ago about the fact that this country economically was gradually, bit by bit, being dominated by another country, that strong steps had to be taken to protect Canadian interests vis-a-vis the invasions of even the friendliest country and in this bill, and certainly in this clause, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, there is no provision that would avoid exorbitant profits and no provision that would prevent any dominant group from any outside jurisdiction coming in and taking control of the situation provided for under clause 44 of this bill.
What the Leader of the Opposition has said was very relevant. What was said by the minister a few moments ago and earlier in the discussion of this bill and particularly on this clause has served to confirm the position that we in this party have taken with regard to foreign participation. The objective of all Canadians, of course, is to see to it that Canadians participate to the full, but in this stage of the development of our country we have not felt it was possible by regulation to take a firm stand in that particular. That was an honest position to take.
What was the position hon. gentlemen opposite took? This country was being dominated by the United States by way of the inflow of capital, by way of management of corporations, and the like. In this very clause the government would have had the opportunity of taking the step that would reveal that once in office the government was prepared to act consistently with these declarations on other occasions. While there is no fundamental issue taken with this clause it does afford us the opportunity of saying to hon. gentlemen opposite, including my hon. friend the genial Minister of Public Works who I think was among those who took strongest issue, that nothing is now being done by the government consistent with the position it took before and particularly during the election with regard to the domination of this country by those who supply capital by way of investment from the United States in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not very difficult to deal with the point raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West who is undoubtedly upset because a particular method put forward by those in that group for meeting this problem has not been found acceptable to those in this party. It is one thing

to complain about the action of the government in these matters in the past and about the weakness of a particular provision but it is something else to introduce a provision which is quite unrealistic, unworkable and which would not accomplish the purpose which even those hon. gentlemen have in mind.
To put in legislation that an applicant must have a certain percentage of the stock held in Canadian hands and to make no provision for any change in stock ownership after that provision has been fulfilled makes no sense at all. You might have 51 per cent of the stock in Canadian hands at the time of the application and a week later only 10 per cent. For the C.C.F. to suggest that this particular problem is solved by this kind of amendment shows how unrealistic they are when it comes down to practical matters.
And now, Mr. Chairman, to turn to important matters, this particular provision does not deal with the question that my hon. friend has dealt with, and which has so often been in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite, especially when they were over here: what can be done to ensure maximum Canadian control of Canadian companies?
I quite appreciate the minister's point that in mentioning tolls in particular I was anticipating perhaps another clause of the bill. But the fact remains that this is the clause in the bill which was put forward by the Prime Minister and others as a clause which would ensure that there should be no unwarranted, exorbitant profits. These are not the exact words he used but I think it is a fair interpretation of what he said. There is nothing in this clause which would necessarily bring about that result at all. All it says is that the board may have regard to the following in issuing a licence:
The financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the line-
So far as I can make out, this is the only provision in this legislation which bears on profits of pipe line companies that the board, before it should give the licence, may take into consideration. To suggest to the committee and to the country that this is a guarantee that there will not be extraordinarily high exorbitant profits, creates an entirely false impression. The government has done nothing whatever in this legislation to implement the expressions they used to use when they were in opposition any more than the C.C.F. have done anything practical in putting forward its amendment to meet this situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

I notice we have passed a clause whereby the board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate for the building of a pipe line or an international power line, and naturally there will be attached to such certificate all kinds of conditions to which the applicant will be expected to adhere. In clause 47, subclause 1; we are being asked to give the board the power of revoking a certificate once issued if in the opinion of the board the person to whom it was issued has violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof. I also notice that once again in

this clause there are the words "with the approval of the governor in council". For the life of me I cannot understand why that phrase should be there.
Once a certificate has been issued upon the recommendation of the board and with the authorization of the governor in council, once the cabinet and the board have agreed upon the necessary terms and conditions, I completely fail to understand why the board should not then have the authority to exercise powers of enforcement with respect to the terms and conditions under which the certificate was issued. I do not see why the cabinet should want to retain the right to revoke or suspend a certificate. We feel that the powers of policing and the authority to enforce the terms and conditions under which the certificate has been issued should certainly be vested in the board and not in the governor in council. Therefore I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West:
That subsection 1 of section 47 be amended by deleting the words "with the approval of the governor in council''.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR A NATIONAL FLAG OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will allow me to make a few brief remarks about this bill for the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag.
The matter has often been debated, and fairly recently, last February 20, 1959, it was again talked out, but comes up again this afternoon. Much has been said and written about this matter and I hope that the members of the house will limit themselves to brief remarks so that we can vote on that bill.
The Liberal party has been often criticized for its failure in the past to adopt a distinctive flag. In fact, a member of the present government the Solicitor General (Mr. Bal-cer) said, during the 1957 electoral campaign, as reported in the Nouvelliste of May 20, 1957:

Mr. Balcer stated that among concerns dear to French-Canadian hearts were those of a distinctive Canadian flag and of the appointment of an ambassador to the Vatican.
Whenever those matters were raised in the commons, he said, federal members from Quebec remained riveted to their seats until the question was put and then rose only to register their opposition.
It is therefore time that hon. members on government benches take a leaf out of the Solicitor General's book and leap at the chance they now have to state their views by voting for or against a distinctive flag. If they oppose the bill, we will see that it is the party now in power which does not want it.
We often hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) preaching national unity. Only recently, at a banquet in Montreal, he told his audience that he had a surprise in store for them which would reveal the cabinet's attitude while favouring national unity.
By this bill members of the house, particularly those on the government side, are provided with a splendid opportunity to give special attention to the matter. Members of the Conservative party, who profess to belong to the party of national unity, now have a chance to say whether they are in favour of a national flag.
A public survey has been conducted in the larger cities of Canada: Victoria, Vancouver, Edmonton, Saskatoon, Calgary, Toronto, London, Montreal and Saint John, New Brunswick. The result of that survey was published in the Canadian High Life News of January 25, 1958. In that survey, the following question was put to 1,200 students: "Do you think Canada should have its distinctive national flag?" The replies were 83 per cent in favour, 13 per cent against and 3.3 per cent undecided.
This proves once again that the time has come to reach a decision on this matter. If the people in Canada's large cities feel it is time to have a distinctive flag, I say and repeat that it is our duty as representatives of all Canadian citizens, to decide whether the matter of a distinctive flag should be settled today or again put off.
Mr. Speaker, when you see a country as under-developed as Ghana choose a national flag immediately upon being recognized as an independent state, whereas Canada, which contributes to assistance under the Colombo plan and helps underdeveloped countries of the world in their struggle for survival, has no distinctive flag, you cannot help feeling the absurdity of the situation which should be remedied once and for all.

A friend of mine who visited the Brussels fair was telling me that every country represented there was flying a distinctive flag, whereas Canada, if I remember correctly, flew the Red Ensign, the flag of our merchant navy. Such a situation is simply absurd. The more you go into the matter, the more you realize that it should be settled as soon as possible, in the best interest of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of dealing with this matter at any great length, and I urge hon. members to take this opportunity to indicate whether they are for or against the bill under consideration.
In closing my remarks, I ask the house to reach a decision and to put the matter to a vote.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR A NATIONAL FLAG OF CANADA
speechtext:
There is no doubt in my mind that the great majority of Canadians do want their own flag, and this majority has been growing during the years. Undoubtedly two wars have played no small part in influencing Canadians into wanting their own flag, because thousands of young men who went to fight in other lands wanted a symbol of their own national identity. That is what a flag provides-national identification.
I do not blame the Liberal party for not having introduced a national flag during the 22 years when they were in office, but I do think it is a little ridiculous now for them to try to find evidence in favour of a flag when they had ample opportunity in the past to do something about it themselves. None of us in this house wants this flag to become a political issue. We do not want to create a division over something which can be a very emotional matter. What we must do is call upon that well-known Canadian characteristic-compromise. With our two healthy and vocal cultures, we have built our nation through compromise. If there is any controversy over this bill, I do not believe it arises over whether we should have our own flag or not; what we have to agree upon is the design of the flag.
Like all other hon. members I have received hundreds of suggested designs, some of them absolutely monstrosities, other meaningless and still others rather attractive. But a flag is not just a selection of colour and emblems. It is a tracing of history. That is why I believe we should have the Union Jack
National Flag of Canada as our flag. The Union Jack is part of our history. It grew out of British history, which, in turn, is part of Canadian history. In a book called "The History of the Union Jack" by Barlow Cumberland, there is this description of a flag:
National flags are not merely a haphazard patchwork of coloured bunting, nor meaningless things. Their combinations have a history and tell a story.
When we look back on this history of the Union Jack, the story it tells is one of continuous growth. Part of that growth has been provided by Canada. For instance this three-crossed Union Jack of Canada is the only flag on this continent which has always been a flag of liberty, a flag by which all men, as their birthright, have been created free and equal. Other countries, in their past, tolerated slavery, but as soon as a slave reached Canada he was free. That, surely, is a fact that should make us proud.
In most parts of this world today the red ensign with our coat of arms is recognized as the Canadian flag and it seems to us particularly fitting that this should be so. Canada is the senior member of the greatest federation or combination of nations ever seen in the world history

the British commonwealth of nations. In 1901 Australia adopted the blue ensign with six stars as her national flag. New Zealand also has the blue ensign with four stars, and the white ensign as her naval flag. Surely the red ensign, or the white ensign, would be especially fitting for Canada? The white ensign might well be chosen as a distinctive Canadian flag depicting the fact that we are a northern country of snow and forests. But whatever is chosen, whether the flag is red or white or blue, let us not obliterate the Union Jack from the design.
Three arguments are mainly used against the inclusion of the Union Jack. First, it is said that it indicates British sovereignty over Canada; second, that the Union Jack has no symbol in it to represent the French part of our nation; and, third, that the Union Jack means nothing to the ethnic groups in our country. Let us consider these three arguments one by one.
As to the argument that the Union Jack indicates British sovereignty over Canada, I do not believe that any thinking Canadian really holds that view today. In his heart of heart every Canadian knows that Britain has no desire or right or inclination to infringe on our independence, our sovereignty. As to the contention that the Union Jack bears no symbol in it to represent the French part of our nation, that is true, but if our

National Flag of Canada French-speaking Canadians want some symbolic emblem in our new flag, by all means let us have it. If the fleur-de-lys answers that objection, let us have it; if the maple leaf answers it, let us have it. But the fact remains that the Union Jack is still part of Canadian history and it should be in our flag somewhere.
A great Canadian, His Excellency the Governor General, once made a speech which has been put into a book, and the title of his speech was "The Quest for Unity". He had this to say:
The British tradition in Canada has fortified our sense of freedom. Today our association with the other nations of the commonwealth is an expression of political liberty. If it is sometimes said that the British connection is an evidence of "colonial subordination". Nothing could be further from the truth. The "colonial" point of view no longer exists as a factor in our national life, and is held by no thinking Canadian.
Then we are told that the Union Jack has no meaning for those ethnic groups who have come to this country and become Canadians. I cannot accept that argument, either. People from other lands came here by their own choice, knowing that the Union Jack was part of our history. They might well have been influenced by that very fact, because the Union Jack is a symbol of liberty, a flag by which all men, as their birthright, have been created free and equal. As a people I believe we are all too prone to tear down the old for the new and modem. It seems to me that in a rather immature way we appear to want to throw away all our traditions to show how grown up and independent we are.
On Christmas Day, 1957 Her Majesty the Queen in her broadcast issued this warning which I think applies very strongly to us at this particular time in our history in deciding about a flag:
It Is not the new institutions which are the difficulty. Our trouble is caused by unthinking people who carelessly throw away ageless ideals as if they were old and outworn machinery.
I believe that the Union Jack is one of those ageless ideals. It has been the inspiration of many deeds of heroism in Canada by French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians and Canadians from many ethnic groups. I say to this house, let us not throw out this part of our past and of our traditions as if it were old and outworn machinery. Let us have a Canadian flag but let us keep the Union Jack in the design of it.

We have two great cultural groups in this land both with traditions that go back to their homelands in Europe. Those of French Canada were broken by the French revolution but the traditions of English speaking Canada, by chance, were carried forward without interruption. The contribution of French speaking Canada to the growth of this country and the development of our nationalism and to the position we occupy in the world today cannot be over-estimated. After the American revolution and during the war of 1812-14 it was French Canada that was a major bulkwark of defence against aggression.
The history of this country to a great extent up to very recent times has been

the history of Upper and Lower Canada. I for one will pay tribute to the advantage we have had in the contribution of French Canada to maintaining our national integrity. The French culture has acted as a barrier against our absorption into the United States. I resent such remarks as those made by the sponsor in introducing the bill on February 20, at which time he spoke about putting an end to spurious sentiment. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to go into the technicalities of the bill before us. I wish to discuss some of the principles of the matter and express the views of a third group of Canadians, neither English nor French. I think I have the right to reflect their ideas and thoughts; therefore I hope the house will bear with me if I make some remarks along these lines.
The question of a new flag is a very interesting one. We say we have grown up; we are no longer a British colony. But Canadians seem to be divided into three distinct groups on this particular question of a flag. I say there is one section of the country which wants a distinctive Canadian flag and which would eliminate the Union Jack and the fleur-de-lis; that is, we must erase all traces of the past that the Union Jack and the fleur-de-lis have stood for. Another section of our population wants a distinctive Canadian flag but it must have the Union Jack on some part of it. There is another section of our country that considers that discussion of the flag is taboo; it is something we must not discuss because it might hurt somebody's feeling. I feel, that when a matter of public interest cannot be discussed in a free country, that country ceases to be free. Therefore, if I am unduly frank in some of my remarks, I feel that I am in a free country which permits free discussion, and it is something that is our right and privilege.
I would go along with the hon. member for York Humber (Miss Aitken) but not in every respect. I do not wish to be repetitious, but yet I make reference to the fact that our sister nations of the commonwealth, namely Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, above all, have a Union Jack on some part of their flags. I will answer the question. I think Canada should have a distinctive national flag. I am not particular as to what colour it should be, I mean the whole field of it, whether it should be blue, red white or any other colour, but I have strong feelings, about the fact that it should contain a union jack of some kind. I cannot help it; it is in my bringing up. I remember that during the first world war when I attended public school we sang the song "We will never let the old flag fall." I still get a thrill when I think of it. I remember
(Mr. Robichaud.]
the song "Red, white and blue, what does it mean to you". It is ingrained in my generation, and I am neither of French nor Anglo-Saxon origin.
I feel that the Union Jack stands for something and that we just cannot wipe it out. It stands for our solidarity with the British empire, but not as a colony. We are not a colony. We are a sovereign nation voluntarily in the British commonwealth of nations and the Union Jack stands for that solidarity, for that empire. It stands for the tradition of freedom that we enjoy here and that people, whether white, black or yellow, enjoy wherever that flag has been planted, no matter in what part of the world. To me that flag stands as a symbol of the tradition of fair play and the tradition of British justice.
I think various sectors of our population owe a great deal to the Union Jack, and I am going to be quite frank. I have met Canadians of French origin who have confessed to me that the Union Jack meant something to them in that when the Union Jack was planted on the plains of Abraham those who planted it there did not treat them as a conquered people. That flag guaranteed them freedom of culture, freedom of religion, freedom of language and that agreement has been kept to the letter.
What does it mean to one of Anglo-Saxon origin? He brought it with him from his mother land. He brought it from England. What does it mean to the descendants of the United Empire loyalists who came to the Ontario wilderness from the colonies just to be under that flag? Their descendants have a right to their sentiment and it is a ridiculous statement for anyone to say that as a majority want a new distinctive flag the Union Jack must be wiped out altogether. That is a ridiculous statement just as it is a ridiculous statement to say that the ethnic groups which, according to some figures, comprise one-third of our population, want any other flag. I have still to receive a request from any of my fellow Canadians of any ethnic group, including my own, for a new Canadian flag. I do not think that question bothers them at all. They will be happy. Probably the young generation would be happy to have a new distinctive Canadian flag. But, as I have mentioned, there is this sentiment with regard to what the Union Jack stands for.
Some people say that we have no flag today. Yes, we have. The Canadian ensign is our flag. We are going to display it on all public buildings and public places when Her Majesty visits Canada. It is very easy to say that we have grown up but when

my son grew up I did not expect him to throw away my name, the name I gave him. I did not expect him to throw away the traditions in which I brought him up. I did not expect him to forget the language 1 taught him.
Throw away the Union Jack? Why not throw away the idea of Her Majesty being our queen? Why not throw away all the parliamentary procedure we have inherited from the mother of parliaments? Why not throw away all our freedoms? Why not throw away our tradition of justice and fair play?
I am going to make my remarks brief, Mr. Speaker, because I should like to see others state what they feel they should contribute to this debate. But I am going to tell you one thing. When the boat on which my father came to Canada approached these shores he saw that flag and found refuge under it. That applies not only to my father but to millions of immigrants from all parts of the world. To them it meant the same thing as the statue of liberty in New York harbour. It has meant that to them. It meant that to my father because that flag guaranteed him freedom and liberty.
Finally, may I say that I cannot express myself too strongly. I am in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag and I do not care what colour it is. However, I feel very strongly, and I believe there are millions of Canadians who feel the same way I do, that on some part of it the Union Jack must appear. Otherwise we are breaking away from everything we have got. Otherwise we are going to become a satellite of the United States. We will be heading toward becoming the 51st state of the United States. I want to retain our connection with the crown. I want to retain our connection with Britain, not as a servant, not as a subservient colony, but as an equal, and we are treated as such.
We are all looking forward to Her Majesty's visit to Canada. Why, tell me why this should be done. We have the same queen, common laws and common justice. Are we ashamed of that flag? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let my first remarks be an expression of deep sympathy with the former Liberal administration, particularly
National Flag of Canada bearing in mind a resolution passed in January 1958, during a Liberal convention, in favour of a distinctive national flag. Of course, Mr. Speaker, you will appreciate the genuineness of my feelings because, as everybody knows, that wonderful, sincere and firm resolution was adopted by the former administration after having been in power for 22 years in this country.
Mr. Speaker, the matter we are discussing tonight is obviously of a very delicate nature. Thousands of Canadians have quite different opinions on this matter. Some favour an exclusively Canadian flag, others would like to see the past remembered, by leaving on the Canadian flag the Union Jack or the red ensign. Such views must be respected by both sides.
The Union Jack and red ensign should of course be referred to with great respect by all Canadians. Canadians of all racial origins, particularly during the last two wars, have fought under those flags. Many Canadians, of either English or French origin,, dying on the battlefield, looked their last upon this flag which we revere and respect, whatever our origin.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, we must reckon with history, and with the years, and not only years past but years to come. Our nation-as none will gainsay-is still comparatively young. While we are about to celebrate the centennial of Canadian confederation, our history goes back to no more than three or four centuries. This country which is rich in possibilties, both in human capital and natural resources, is destined to play a tremendous part in the future.
If Canadians, whose predecessors started to consolidate the national unity in 1867 with the confederative pact, want to continue that work of consolidation, I believe that Canada should choose an exclusively Canadian flag, a distinctive flag.
Of course, in this country where I believe we enjoy a greater measure of freedom than in any other, a Canadian citizen-whether a Canadian-born or naturalized citizen-must be entitled to the same rights and privileges, whatever his origin.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to those two great races, the French and English, that pioneered this country, there are thousands of Canadians who have lived in this land for many generations. Some of them already form large racial groups that are worthy of respect.
What would happen then if each of those racial groups, already large and deserving

National Flag of Canada of regard, should want to place on the Canadian flag the emblems of their own origins? It would of course lead to a practically inextricable situation. Each group would have excellent reasons for wanting on the Canadian flag an emblem reminding them of their origin.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that we should forget the glories of the past. Canadians of English origin, and Canadians of French origin have both played a significant part in the history of our country. But we must consider that Canada, being a young country, must look above all toward the future. It is for that reason, most of all, that in making these remarks in the house tonight, I say I am in favour of the adoption of an exclusively Canadian flag.
Before resuming my seat, I should like to stress again all the respect, admiration and veneration I have for our history. Our country has already glorious pages of history to its credit, but how many more remain to be written about this country, Canada, which today is considered as an adult country by other nations. I believe that we should be in a position to display at international gatherings, a flag which would clearly assert our independence, our will to grow and to progress. That does not necessarily exclude, Mr. Speaker, the reproduction on a Canadian flag of a certain emblem denoting the origins of the two great races which presided over the foundation of the country in which we are proud to live today.

I am sure that, like other hon. members, my heart swells with pride because as a member from British Columbia this has been my flag. I think many people in Canada have recognized it as their flag.
Perhaps there should be a little more recognition given to the French background
of a great part of our nation, but I feel that will come about in the course of time. I do not believe that by any stretch of the imagination a flag is going to make a nation of us. We first have to become a nation, and then we will evolve a flag, a flag which truly represents the nation of Canada. It is rather a coincidence that I am following my good friend the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere). I have had the pleasure of visiting him in Quebec city on two different occasions. I must say that I did not feel I was outside of Canada when I saw the fleur-de-lis flying from many of the buildings. I am sure that when they come to western Canada they do not feel that they are outside of Canada.
I believe that this whole question, Mr. Speaker, of a distinctive national flag will resolve itself as we become more and more a nation.
